metadata.title: Congress Doesn't Beat the Market. The Cluster Does.
metadata.note: CLI video in the REQUIRED spine: B00 cold open (ClaudeComposerAsk, ask answered) · B01 PROBLEM (STOCK Act, 13,877 trades, the copy-Congress question) · B02 ASK · B03 CODE (market_adjusted.py, the ACTUAL code) · B04 OUTPUT(manim, aggregate alpha +0.13%) · B05 CHANGE (cluster tiering revision) · B06 CODE (backtest.py tag_signal) · B07 OUTPUT(manim, tier table) · B08 SUMMARY (manim recap) · B09 NEXT STEPS (handoff, 'Your turn.') · B10 outro (ClaudeTitleOutro). beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW — open on the Claude UI, ask shown answered; IN-FOR-BEAR LAW in narration
beats.narration_text: Namaste — this is Liam, in for Ameya. Build it with Claude, then take it apart. Today: thirteen thousand congressional stock trades, and the one signal inside them that isn't noise.

props.command: claude "backtest 13,877 congressional stock-trade disclosures — does copying Congress beat the market?"
output: aggregate BUY alpha: +0.13% — Congress rides the market
cluster buys: +0.23% to +0.54% — the only tier above noise

beats.role_note: the stakes BEFORE the build; SHOW-DON'T-TELL — timeline + counters move
beats.narration_text: Since twenty-twelve, the STOCK Act has forced every member of Congress to disclose their stock trades within forty-five days. A law meant to deter insider trading quietly produced a public dataset of what powerful people do with their own money. I scraped it: thirteen thousand, eight hundred and seventy-seven trades from one hundred and eight members, across three years of filings. The popular story says Congress beats the market — whole apps exist to copy them trade for trade. So here is the narrow, testable question: follow every congressional buy mechanically, and do you beat the index?
beats.visual_intent: Manim: STOCK Act timeline (2012 → disclose within 45 days), stat cards animating in (13,877 trades · 108 members · May 2023–Jun 2026), then the question line in terracotta

beats.role_note: composer (ClaudeComposerAsk) — show and discuss the prompt
beats.narration_text: Ask for the strict version of the test. Into Claude: write market underscore adjusted dot pie. For every trade, measure the stock's return over the thirty days after the disclosure date — the first day a retail investor could actually act — and subtract SPY's return over the identical window. That subtraction is the whole methodology: a stock that merely rose with the index shows zero alpha.

props.command: claude "write market_adjusted.py — for each trade: 30-day return from the DISCLOSURE date minus SPY over the identical window; per-trade alpha, no look-ahead"

beats.role_note: ClaudeCodeBeat — ACTUAL-CODE LAW: real lines from market_adjusted.py, trimmed to what teaches
beats.narration_text: Read the code before trusting the result. One function fetches SPY at disclosure, and SPY thirty days later — the same window the trade gets. Then one line does the judging: abnormal return equals the stock's post-disclosure move, minus SPY's. No annualizing, no portfolio smoothing. Every single trade is benchmarked against the market it actually traded in.

props.title: market_adjusted.py
props.code:
# market_adjusted.py — per-trade alpha vs SPY
def compute_spy_return(disclosure_date):
    """SPY return over the SAME 30-day window."""
    spy_at   = get_spy_close(disclosure_date)
    post_dt  = disclosure_date + timedelta(days=30)
    spy_post = get_spy_close(post_dt)
    return round((spy_post - spy_at) / spy_at * 100, 4)

valid['spy_return_30d']  = valid['disclosure_date'].map(spy_returns)
valid['abnormal_return'] = (valid['pct_change_post_disclosure']
                            - valid['spy_return_30d']).round(4)

beats.role_note: OPEN vox slot → Manim video; numbers from RESEARCH_REPORT.md §4.1
beats.narration_text: Run it on five thousand, one hundred and sixty-two priced buys. Raw return: plus two point two three percent — at first glance, Congress can pick stocks. Then the subtraction lands: SPY made plus two point one zero over the same windows. Alpha, plus zero point one three percent. Sells: essentially zero. In aggregate, Congress doesn't beat the market. Congress IS the market, with a rounding error on top.
beats.visual_intent: Manim: paired bars — congressional BUY raw +2.23% vs SPY +2.10% growing to near-identical heights; the +0.13% alpha residual isolated as a sliver; SELL −0.01% noted; verdict line 'Congress rides the market.'

beats.role_note: composer (ClaudeComposerAsk) — THE REVISION LAW; SPARK-LINE LAW greeting 'The revision,'
beats.narration_text: But an average this flat can still hide structure. The revision: stop scoring trades alone, and look for convergence. Update the backtest: flag every buy where two or more members bought the same ticker inside a thirty-day window. Score it with entry-time information only — cluster size, times the group's maximum buy-conviction ratio — and tier every trade before its return is known. No look-ahead: the tier is fixed on the day you could have acted.

props.command: claude "update backtest.py — tier every BUY at entry: cluster = ≥2 politicians, same ticker, 30-day window; signal_score = cluster_size × max BCR; report alpha + win rate per tier"

beats.role_note: ClaudeCodeBeat — real tag_signal lines from backtest.py; the diff that matters is entry-time-only tiering
beats.narration_text: The cluster test is a filter on disclosure dates: same ticker, thirty days either side, count the distinct politicians. The score multiplies that count by the most buy-heavy member's conviction ratio. And the honest part is what the tier function never touches: the realized return. Strong, watch, skip, solo — every tier is assigned from what a reader of the filings would have known at entry.

props.title: backtest.py — tag_signal()
props.code:
# tier from ENTRY-TIME info only — never the return
same   = buys[buys["tkr"] == row["tkr"]]
lo, hi = row["disc_dt"] - timedelta(days=30), \
         row["disc_dt"] + timedelta(days=30)
window = same[(same["disc_dt"] >= lo) & (same["disc_dt"] <= hi)]
pols   = window["politician"].unique()
score  = len(pols) * max(bcr.get(p, 0.5) for p in pols)

def tier(r):
    if r["cluster_size"] < 2:    return "SOLO"
    if r["signal_score"] >= 2.0: return "STRONG"
    if r["signal_score"] >= 1.0: return "WATCH"
    return "SKIP"

beats.role_note: OPEN vox slot → Manim video; numbers from RESEARCH_REPORT.md §4.2
beats.narration_text: Re-run, and the table splits. Clustered buys — strong and watch, about two thousand events — earn positive alpha: plus zero point two three, and plus zero point five four percent, winning just over half the time. Solo buys — three thousand of them — go negative, and win about forty-five percent. That five-point win-rate gap, across five thousand events, is the most robust result in the study. Ten thousand dollars spread across the strong tier finishes at ten thousand two hundred and forty-seven — twenty-three dollars ahead of the same money in SPY. Real, and tiny.
beats.visual_intent: Manim: tier table animating row by row — STRONG n=815 α+0.23% win 50.3% · WATCH n=1,212 α+0.54% win 50.6% · SKIP n=132 α−0.04% win 44.7% · SOLO n=3,003 α−0.05% win 44.9%; clustered rows boxed; bottom line: the ~5-point win gap

beats.role_note: the lesson in one beat — Manim recap, moving per SHOW-DON'T-TELL
beats.narration_text: So what did the build actually show? The edge lives in cluster membership — independent members converging on one ticker — not in the conviction weighting: watch beat strong, so the score adds no ranking power inside a cluster. And one warning from the process: on sixty-four members, the effect looked inverted. It only stabilized at a hundred and eight. This signal is a noise filter, not a profit engine — its real value is the ninety-five percent of trades it tells you to ignore. Research, not investment advice.
beats.visual_intent: Manim: three verdict rows animating with check/cross marks — cluster membership ✓ carries the edge; conviction score ✗ doesn't rank (WATCH +0.54 > STRONG +0.23); small samples ✗ (64 members inverted → stable at 108); closing line 'a noise filter, not a profit engine'

beats.role_note: HANDOFF LAW — suggested prompt typed in, read aloud and discussed
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Take this prompt: pull the last ninety days of congressional buy disclosures, find every ticker with two or more distinct buyers inside a thirty-day window, and compare each cluster's thirty-day return to SPY. It's worth running because it tests the one claim that mattered here — that convergence, not congressional genius, is where the signal lives — on filings that didn't exist when this video was made.

props.command: claude "pull the last 90 days of congressional BUY disclosures, find tickers with ≥2 distinct buyers in a 30-day window, and compare each cluster's 30-day return to SPY"
